label: sat_func
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{sat_func}
    Let $G$ be an oriented graph. We denote by $\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,G)$ the minimum number of edges in an oriented graph $H$ on $n$ vertices that does not contain a copy of $G$, but adding any new edge to $H$ introduces a copy of $G$.

name: Saturation

label: ssat_func
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{ssat_func}
    Let $G$ be an oriented graph. We denote by $\mathrm{ssat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,G)$ the minimum number of edges in an oriented graph $H$ on $n$ vertices such that adding any new edge to $H$ introduces a new copy of $G$.

label: ssat < sat
title: Observation
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $G$ be an oriented graph, and $v$ be an isolated vertex. If $n > |V(G)|$, then 
    \[\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n, G) = \mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n, G + v) \text{ and } \mathrm{ssat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n, G) = \mathrm{ssat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n, G + v).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $n > |V(G)|$ and let $H_n$ be a graph that has $n$ vertices and $\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n, G)$ edges, such that it avoids $G$, and adding any new edge to $H_n$ introduces a copy of $G$. If $H_n$ avoids $G$, then it also avoids $G + v$. Moreover, if we add an edge $u_1u_2$ to $H_n$, denote by $G'$ the copy of $G$. Then there exists $u \in V(H_n) \setminus V(G')$ such that $G' + u$ is a copy of $G + v$.
    
    This proves $\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n, G) \geq \mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n, G + v)$ and $\mathrm{ssat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n, G) \geq \mathrm{ssat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n, G + v)$. We can repeat the same argument for the opposite direction.
head: environment

label: dichotomy_isolated_edge
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{dichotomy_isolated_edge}
    For every oriented graph $G$ that has an isolated edge, we have
    \[\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n, G) = O(1) \text{ or } \Theta(n).\]
    If $G$ does not contain isolated edges, then 
    \[\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n, G) \geq \mathrm{ssat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n, G) = \Omega(n).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We want to prove that for any $G$ we have
    $\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n, G + e) = O(1) \text{ or } \Theta(n).$ Let $k=|V(G)|.$
    To prove a linear upper bound, it suffices to take as a host graph $G$ and $n-k$ isolated vertices. Adding an edge between two isolated vertices introduces a copy of $G+e$. Then we keep adding edges in the rest of the graph without introducing a copy of $G + e$ until we can. At the end, in the worst case, the number of edges in the host graph is equal to $\binom{n}{2} - \binom{n-k}{2} \leq kn$.
    
    If we assume that the saturation function of $G+e$ is sublinear, then for a large enough $n_0$, there is a host graph on $n_0$ vertices with at least two isolated vertices. These two isolated vertices can be replaced by any number of isolated vertices while preserving the saturation property. Therefore, if the saturation function is not linear, it must be bounded.

    Suppose now that $G$ has no isolated edges. Then, adding an isolated edge to the host graph $H$, no new copy of $G$ is created. This shows that the semisaturation function of $G$ is at least $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: For every unordered graph~\cite{KaszonyiTuza86}, ordered bipartite graph~\cite{FulekKeszegh21}, and vertex-ordered graph~\cite{boskesz023}, the saturation function is either bounded or linear.

label: ssat_bounded
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{ssat_bounded}
    Let $G$ be an oriented graph that contains an isolated edge. Then \[\mathrm{ssat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,G) = O(1).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\overrightarrow{uv}$ be an isolated edge in $G$.
    Let $H$ be the oriented graph on $n$ vertices, which consists of the disjoint union of three copies of the graph $G \setminus \{u, v\}$, with the remaining vertices being isolated. If we take any two non-connected vertices in $H$ and connect them with an oriented edge, then one of the three copies of $G \setminus \{u, v\}$ contains none of the endvertices of this new edge. Thus, a new copy of $G$ is created. Since $H$ has a bounded number of edges, we conclude that $\mathrm{ssat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,G) = O(1)$.
head: environment

label: ssat_n
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{dichotomy_isolated_edge}, it suffices to prove the linear upper bound.

    Let $N_G(u) \setminus \{v\} =\{u_1, u_2, ..., u_s\}$ and $N_G(v) \setminus \{u\} = \{v_1, v_2, \dots, v_t\}$, and assume $r = |V(G)|$. Let $H'$ be the graph obtained by taking the union of $G \setminus \{u, v\}$ and $n-r+2$ isolated vertices, which we denote by $\{w_1, w_2, ..., w_{n-r+2}\}$. Now, we construct the host graph $H$ by adding an edge $\overrightarrow{u_iw_j}$ for all $j \in \{1, \dots, n-r+2\}$, if $\overrightarrow{u_iu} \in E(G)$. Otherwise, we add the edges $\overrightarrow{w_ju_i}$ if $\overrightarrow{u u_i} \in E(G)$. We repeat the same procedure for all $i \in \{1, \dots, s\}$. Then, we repeat it for the vertices $\{v_1, \dots, v_t\}$, adding an edge $\overrightarrow{v_iw_j}$ whenever $\overrightarrow{v_iv} \in E(G)$ or an edge $\overrightarrow{w_jv_i}$ if $\overrightarrow{vv_i} \in E(G)$. Note that we can have $\{u_1, u_2, ..., u_s\} \cap \{v_1, v_2, ..., v_t\} \neq \varnothing$, but by the assumption, the orientation of each new edge is uniquely determined.
    
    Since adding any non-edge in $\{w_1, w_2, ..., w_{n-r+2}\}$ as an edge can have the role of the edge $\overrightarrow{uv}$ in a new copy of $G$, we conclude that $H$ semisaturates $G$.

label: claim:bipdense
title: Claim
body_md:
\cite{boskesz026} \label{claim:bipdense}
	Let $G$ be a graph with at most $cn^{2-\epsilon}$ missing edges, where $c,\epsilon > 0$ are constants, and let $\cal B$ be a bipartite covering of $G$. Then there exists a vertex that is incident to edges belonging to at least $c' \log n$ bipartite graphs in $\cal B$, where $c'$ depends only on $c$ and $\epsilon$.
head: environment

label: ssat_nlogn
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first proceed with the upper bound. Take $\overrightarrow{uv} \in E(G)$ and let $N_G(u) \setminus \{v\} =\{u_1, u_2, ..., u_s\}$ and $N_G(v) \setminus \{u\} = \{v_1, v_2, ..., v_t\}$. We construct a host graph $H$ as a disjoint union of $k$ copies of the graph $G^{uv} = G \setminus \{u,v\}$ and $n'$ isolated vertices denoted by $W = \{w_1, w_2, \dots, w_{n'}\}$, where $k \ge 2 \lceil \log n' \rceil$. We can choose $k$ such that $k=O(\log n)$.

    We can now find $k$ different bipartitions of the set $W$ such that any pair of vertices is separated in at least two of them. For $i \in \{1, \dots, k\}$, we can take one bipartition $(U_i, V_i)$ of the set $W$ and one of the copies of $G^{uv}$ which we denote by $G_{i}^{uv}$. If a vertex is in the set $U_i$, then we connect it with the vertices $\{u_1, \dots, u_s\}$ of the copy $G_{i}^{uv}$ using the same orientations as $u$ is connected to the vertices $\{u_1, \dots, u_s\}$ in $G$. If a vertex is in the set $V_i$, then we connect it with the vertices $\{v_1, \dots, v_t\}$ of the copy $G_{i}^{uv}$ using the same orientation as $v$ is connected to the vertices $\{v_1, \dots, v_t\}$ in $G$. For the same $(U_i, V_i)$, we take another copy of $G^{uv}$ and do the same by switching the role of $U_i$ and $V_i$.
    
    If we add a new edge to $H$, such that one vertex is in $U_i$ and the other is in $V_i$, oriented towards the vertex in $V_i$, then together with the copy $G_{i}^{uv}$, we obtain a new copy of $G$. If it is oriented towards the vertex in $U_i$, then together with the other copy of  $G^{uv}$, we obtain a new copy of $G$.
    Since any two vertices in $W$ are separated in at least one bipartition, it follows that for any new edge, the host graph $H$ semisaturates $G$. This shows that
    \[\mathrm{ssat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n, G) = O(n \log n).\]
    
    \smallskip
    
    We continue with the lower bound. Let $H$ be a saturation host graph on $n$ vertices. For a pair of vertices $f=\{u,v\}$ that do not span an edge of $H$, adding an edge at $f$ in any orientation creates a copy of $G$. Recall that for every edge in $G$ there exists the required $w$. Thus, independently of which edge of $G$ corresponds to $f$, there is a vertex $\pi(f) \in V(H)$ such that either 
    \[\{\overrightarrow{u\pi(f)}, \overrightarrow{\pi(f)v}\} \subset E(H) \text{ or } \{\overrightarrow{v\pi(f)},\overrightarrow{\pi(f)u}\} \subset E(H).\] 
    If multiple such vertices exist, we set $\pi(f)$ to be one of them arbitrarily. For a given vertex $t\in V(H)$, consider the set of all non-edges $f$ with $\pi(f)=t$.
    Observe that $f$ must connect a vertex in $N_G^{in}(t)$ to a vertex in $N_G^{out}(t)$, the neighbors of $t$ that have an edge towards $t$ and away from $t$, respectively. Thus, there is a bipartition of the neighbors of $t$ in $H$ such that every non-edge in $\pi^{-1}(t)$ is between the two parts of this bipartition.
		
	Assume on the contrary that $H$ has less than $cn{\log n}$ edges for some $c\le 1$ chosen later. The non-edges of $H$ must be covered by the sets of non-edges $\pi^{-1}(t)$ where $t$ is a vertex of $H$. As each $\pi^{-1}(t)$ is bipartite, we can apply Claim \ref{claim:bipdense} on the complement of $H$. First, we choose constants $c_0,\epsilon_0$ independently of $c$ such that \[ n\log n\le c_0(n/2)^{2-\epsilon_0}.\] Now we can apply Claim \ref{claim:bipdense} with $c_0,\epsilon_0$.		
	We get that there is a vertex $v$ in $H$ which participates in at least $c'\log n$ many bipartitions that cover the non-edges of $H$. For each $t$ such that $\pi^{-1}(t)$ contains a non-edge $f$ with $\pi(f)=t$ and whose one endpoint is $v$, there is an edge in $H$ from $t$ to both vertices of $f$, and thus to $v$ as well. Thus $v$ is connected to at least $c'\log n$ different such vertices, therefore, to at least $c'\log n$ vertices in $H$.
    
    Delete $v$ from $H$ and repeat this procedure $n/2$ times. In each step we can apply Claim \ref{claim:bipdense} with the same $c_0$ and $\epsilon_0$ to find and delete a vertex with degree at least $c'\log (n/2)$. Altogether, we have found at least $\frac{n}{2} c'\log (n/2)$ edges in $H$. When $c$ is small enough this contradicts our assumption that $H$ has less than $cn\log n$ edges (note that $c'$ was independent from $c$).

label: cor:subsat
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:subsat}
    Let $G$ be an oriented graph such that for each edge $\overrightarrow{uv} \in E$ there exists $w \in N_G(u) \cap N_G(v)$, such that either $\{\overrightarrow{uw}, \overrightarrow{wv}\} \subset E$ or $\{\overrightarrow{vw},\overrightarrow{wu}\} \subset E$. Let $H$ be a graph with vertex set $V=V_1\cup V_2$ such that for every non-edge of $V_2$ adding this edge would create a new copy of $G$ in $H$. Then $H$ has $\Omega(|V_2|\log |V_2|)$ edges.

label: cor:triangles
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:triangles}
Let $G$ be an oriented graph such that every edge is in some oriented triangle. Then \[\mathrm{ssat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,G) = \Theta(n \log n).\]

label: k4_bounded
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{k4_bounded}
    Let $G$ be an oriented graph on $k$ vertices such that $\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,G + e) = O(1)$. Then, its host graph with $n$ vertices and $\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,G + e)$ edges has at most $k^2$ non-isolated vertices. Consequently, $\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,G + e) = O(k^4)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $H$ be a host graph with a bounded number of edges and fix an isolated vertex $v$. If we connect it to another isolated vertex, we obtain in the rest of $H$ a copy of $G$, which we denote by $G'$. Since $H$ is $(G+e)$-free, $V(H) \setminus V(G')$ spans an independent set. Therefore, every edge in $H$ contains at least one vertex in $G'$.

    Let $u \in V(G')$ and add the edge $\overrightarrow{uv}$ to $H$. We then obtain a copy of $G+e$, which has at most $k-1$ non-isolated vertices outside of $G'$. Indeed, if $\overrightarrow{uv}$ plays the role of the isolated edge $e$, then at least one vertex of the copy of $G$ must be in $G'$, so at most $k-1$ of its vertices lie outside $V(G')$. On the other hand, if $\overrightarrow{uv}$ plays the role of an edge from $G$, then there are at most $k-2$ vertices of $G$ and one vertex of $e$ outside of $G'$, as desired.
    
    By repeating this argument for every vertex in $G'$, we get at most $k(k-1)$ vertices outside $V(G')$. Altogether, there are at most $k^2$ non-isolated vertices, including $V(G')$.
head: environment

label: r+1 noniso
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{r+1 noniso}
    Let $T$ be a tournament on $r\ge 2$ vertices. If $\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,T + e) = O(1)$, then for large enough $n$, its host graphs with $n$ vertices and $\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,T + e)$ edges have exactly $r+1$ non-isolated vertices that span a tournament, and every subset of $r$ vertices of this tournament spans a copy of $T$. Consequently, $\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,T + e) = \binom{r+1}{2}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $H$ be a host graph with a bounded number of edges. By assumption, there exists a subgraph $T' \subset H$ that is isomorphic to $T$. If the host graph has at most $r$ non-isolated vertices, then it cannot saturate edges between an isolated vertex and a non-isolated vertex.
    Note that the vertices $V(H)\setminus V(T')$ must span an independent set, therefore any copy of $T$ can have at most one vertex from this set.

    Fix an isolated vertex $w$. For every $u \in V(T')$, adding the edge $\overrightarrow{uw}$ creates a copy of $T + e$ such that $T$ is isomorphic to the graph spanned over the vertices of $T'-u$ and one of the vertices $v_u \notin V(T')$. 

    If for every $u\in V(T')$ these $v_u$ vertices are all the same, then we get a tournament on $r+1$ vertices such that every subset of $r$ vertices spans a copy of $T$. Notice that there are no further edges in the graph, as we would then get a copy of $T+e$.

    Otherwise, assume there exist $u, u' \in V(T')$ such that $v_u\ne v_{u'}$. In this case, $v_u$ is connected to every vertex of $T'-u$, thus also to $u'$. The edge between $u'$ and $v_u$ together with the copy of $T$ on $V(T'-u')\cup \{v_{u'}\}$ forms a copy of $T+e$, which is a contradiction.
head: environment

label: subgraph of a tournament
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{subgraph of a tournament}
    Let $T$ be a tournament on $r$ vertices, and let $S$ be a spanning subgraph of $T$. If $\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,T + e) = O(1)$, then $\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,S + e) = O(1)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By Lemma \ref{r+1 noniso} large enough host graphs $H$ of $T+e$ have at most $r+1$ non-isolated vertices. Therefore, they also do not contain $S$, which has $r+2$ non-isolated vertices. On the other hand, adding any edge to $H$ introduces a copy of $T+e$, and thus also of $S+e$.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
We observe that Lemmas \ref{k4_bounded} and \ref{r+1 noniso}, together with the dichotomy obtained in Lemma \ref{dichotomy_isolated_edge}, provide an algorithmic characterization of the saturation functions of oriented graphs of the form $G+e$. Namely, if $G$ has $k$ vertices, we can check all oriented graphs on $n$ vertices with at most $k^2$ non-isolated vertices to determine whether any of them saturates $G+e$. If such a graph exists, then the algorithm also determines the exact saturation function. Otherwise, we conclude that the saturation function is linear. Note that this algorithm is exponential in $k$. 
    
    For a tournament $T$, this algorithm can be simplified. It suffices to take a copy of $T$ and add a single vertex, considering every possible orientation of the edges between this vertex and the vertices of $T$.
head: environment
name: Algorithmic characterization

label: claim:e+acyclic
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{claim:e+acyclic}
    Let $G$ be an acyclic oriented graph. Then \[\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,G + e) = O(1).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Assume $G$ has $k \geq 2$ vertices. Then we take a host graph $H$ to be a transitive tournament on $k+1$ vertices, and the remaining $n-k-1$ vertices are isolated. Since $|V(H)| < |V(G+e)|$, $H$ avoids $G+e$. Let $u, v \in V(H)$ be such that $uv \notin E(H)$. Then we can assume that one of them is isolated, say $u$. Now, we can observe that $H - v$ contains a transitive tournament of size $k$. Therefore, since $G$ is a spanning subgraph of a transitive tournament, $H - v$ also contains $G$. By taking $e = uv$, we conclude that $H + uv$ contains $G + e$.
head: environment

title: Claim
body_md: Let $T$ be a tournament with outdegree sequence $d_1 \leq d_2 \leq \dots \leq d_r$. If there exists $k \in \{1, \dots, r-1\}$ such that $d_k + 2 \leq d_{k+1}$, then \[\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,T + e) = \Theta(n).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{r+1 noniso}, it suffices to show that there is no tournament $T_{r+1}$ on $r+1$ vertices such that any subset of $r$ vertices induces a copy of $T$. Suppose such a tournament $T_{r+1}$ exists. Choose one vertex $u$, and label the remaining $r$ vertices $v_1, \dots, v_r$ so that they induce a copy of $T$ in which $v_i$ has outdegree $d_i$.

    Moreover, $T_{r+1}-v_k$ must induce a copy of $T$. We get this from the earlier copy of $T$ by removing $v_k$ and adding $u$. Note that no $v_i$ with $i > k$ can play the role of a vertex $v_j$ with $j \leq k$, since deleting a single vertex decreases the outdegree of every remaining vertex by at most one. Therefore, after removing $v_k$, the vertex $u$ must play the role of a vertex with outdegree at most $d_k$. Consequently, $d^+(u)\le d_k+1$.
    
    Similarly, in the copy of $T$ induced by $T_{r+1}-v_{k+1}$, the vertex $u$ must correspond to a vertex with outdegree at least $d_{k+1}$. In particular, $d^+(u)\geq d_{k+1}$.
    We get that \[d_{k+1}\le d^+(u)\leq d_k+1<d_{k+1},\] 
    a contradiction.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: An oriented graph $G$ is \emph{deletion-homogeneous} if, for any pair of vertices $u, v$, the graphs $G - u$ and $G - v$ are isomorphic.
head: environment

title: Claim
body_md: Let $r \geq 1$ and let $G$ be a deletion-homogeneous graph on $r+1$ vertices. If $G'$ is a subgraph of $G$ on $r$ non-isolated vertices, then $\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,G' + e) = O(1)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We can take a host graph $H$ of $G' + e$ to be $G$ and $n-r-1$ isolated vertices. Since $G' + e$ has $r+2$ non-isolated vertices, it is certainly avoided by this construction. Furthermore, by assumption, $G$ is deletion homogeneous, so $G - v$ is isomorphic to $G'$ for any vertex $v$. We conclude that by adding any edge $uv$, where $u$ is an isolated vertex of $H$, we introduce a copy of $G' + e$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Let $G_1$ and $G_2$ be two oriented graphs. We denote by $G_1 \circ G_2$ the oriented graph obtained by replacing every vertex of $G_1$ with a copy of $G_2$, and if $\overrightarrow{uv} \in E(G_1)$ then $\overrightarrow{u'v'} \in E(G_1 \circ G_2)$ for all $u' \in G_2^u$ and $v' \in G_2^v$, where $G_2^u$ and $G_2^v$ are the copies of $G_2$ that replace $u$ and $v$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md: Let $G_1$ be a vertex-transitive graph and $G_2$ be a deletion-homo\-geneous graph. Then $G_1 \circ G_2$ is a deletion-homogeneous graph.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $v_1, v_2 \in V(G_1 \circ G_2)$, and let $G'_2$ and $G''_2$ be two disjoint copies of $G_2$ in $G_1 \circ G_2$. We can distinguish two cases.
    
    First, suppose $v_1, v_2 \in V(G'_2)$. Then we can see that $G_1 \circ G_2 - v_1$ and $G_1 \circ G_2 - v_2$ are isomorphic because the graph $G_2$ is deletion-homogeneous and the isomorphism is given by swapping the roles of $v_1$ and $v_2$, while keeping the  other vertices the same. 
    
    Second, suppose $v_1 \in V(G'_2)$ and $v_2 \in V(G''_2)$. Since $G_2$ is deletion-homogeneous, we can find an isomorphism between $G'_2 - v_1$ and $G''_2 - v_2$. By the assumption that $G_1$ is vertex-transitive, we conclude that $G_1 \circ G_2 - v_1$ and $G_1 \circ G_2 - v_1$ are isomorphic.
head: environment

label: acyc_linear
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{dichotomy_isolated_edge}, we only need an upper bound construction.
    We define a host graph $H$ on the vertex set $\{v_1, \dots, v_n\}$. Starting with the empty graph, we add edges one-by-one in the following way. We take the first vertex $v_1$ and keep adding edges $\overrightarrow{v_1v_j}$ for $1 < j \leq n$ either until a copy of $G$ is created (in which case we do not add this last edge) or $j=n$. Then we do the same for further vertices $v_2,v_3,\dots$ one-by-one. In a general step, we add edges from some $v_i$ to $v_j$ with $i<j\leq n$ until a copy of $G$ is created (in which case we do not add this last edge) or $j=n$.
    
    This procedure stops (that is, adds no more edges) at some vertex $v_x$ after adding $y\ge 0$ edges $v_xv_j$ with $x<j< n$. First, $x\le k-1$, otherwise when we add the edge $\overrightarrow{v_{k-1}v_k}$, a copy of the transitive tournament on $k$ vertices is created, which contains $G$. Next, $y< k$, otherwise in the last step, when adding the edge $\overrightarrow{v_{x}v_{x+y+1}}$, we would create a copy of $G$, necessarily using the new vertex $v_{x+y+1}$. However, the vertices $v_{x+1},\dots v_{x+y}$ all have the same neighborhoods as $v_{x+y+1}$ would have. Thus, we could replace $v_{x+y+1}$ in this copy of $G$ by one of $v_{x+1},\dots,v_{x+y}$ that does not belong to the copy (which is possible since $y\ge k$), showing that a copy of $G$ already existed before the last step.

    We obtain a graph $H_0$ with at most $(k-1)n$ edges such that adding any further edge incident to $v_x$ oriented away from $v_x$ creates a graph $H_0'$ containing $G$. 
    We now greedily extend $H_0$ until it saturates $G$. Let $H$ denote this graph.
    Note that in $H$, no vertex $v_i$, $i>x$ can have an out-degree larger than $y$, as otherwise this vertex could play the role of $v_x$ in a copy of $H_0'$ (while all other vertices are the same) and therefore would also contain $G$. Thus, as $y< k$, we added at most $(k-1)n$ further edges.

    Therefore, the saturation function of $G$ is at most $2(k-1)n$, which completes the proof.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: It suffices to use Claim \ref{claim:e+acyclic} and Lemma \ref{acyc_linear} to obtain a full characterization of saturation functions for acyclic oriented graphs.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $G$ be an oriented graph that contains a unique vertex $x \in V(G)$ with indegree (or outdegree) zero. Then
    \[\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,G) \leq \mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,G - x) + O(n).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We take a host graph $H_{G-x}$ of $G-x$ on $n-1$ vertices. To obtain a host graph $H$ of $G$, we add a vertex $v$ to $H_{G-x}$ and add an edge $v \rightarrow u$ for all $u \in V(H_{G-x})$. 
    First, assume that $H(G)$ contains $G$. As $H_{G-x}$ avoids $G$, the only way for $H(G)$ to contain a copy of $G$ is to have $v$ in it. Since $v$ has a zero indegree, it can only have the role of the vertex $x$. That would mean $H_{G-x}$ contains a copy of $G-x$, which is not possible. Second, $H(G)$ saturates $G$ because $H_{G-x}$ saturates $G-x$.
head: environment

label: ver_trans
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{ver_trans}
    Let $G$ be a vertex-transitive graph, and let $G_1$ and $G_2$ be connected subgraphs of $G$. If $|V(G_1)|+|V(G_2)| \geq |V(G)|+1$, then 
    \[\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n, F) = \Theta(n),\]
    for every $F \in G_1 \rightarrow G_2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As $F$ is a connected graph, its saturation function is at least linear. On the other hand, we can construct a host graph by taking linearly many disjoint copies of $G$. Note that $F$ is connected and has more vertices than $G$. Thus, we obtain that each copy of $G$ avoids $G_1 \rightarrow G_2$, and therefore the host graph does so too.
    
    It remains to show that this graph is saturated. If we add an edge between two different copies of $G$, then, by vertex-transitivity, we can find a copy of $G_1$ in one of them and a copy of $G_2$ in the other. Together with the added edge, they form a copy of $F$.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $G$ be a vertex-transitive graph. Let $G_1$ be a spanning subgraph of $G$, and $G_2$ a connected subgraph of $G$. Then
    \[\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n, F) = \Theta(n),\]
    for every $F \in G_1 \rightarrow G_2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: It suffices to observe that $|V(G)| = |V(G_1)|$, and so the inequality from Lemma \ref{ver_trans} is satisfied.
head: environment

label: sat_nlogn
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The lower bound follows from Lemma \ref{ssat_nlogn}.
    For the upper bound, we use the same host construction $H$ as the one provided in the proof of Lemma \ref{ssat_nlogn} using $\overrightarrow{xy}$ as the distinguished edge. However, we apply the construction to only one of the largest connected components of $G$. It remains to show that this construction indeed avoids the oriented graph $G$.
    
    We assume the contrary and notice that any copy should contain at least one edge incident to the vertex set $W$ (the independent set defined in the construction). Indeed, in $H-W$ there are not enough components of $G$ of the largest size to contain a copy of $G$. So, assume there is a vertex $w \in W$ in the copy of $G$. Notice that by the assumption, $N_H(w)$ forms an independent set since it inherits the neighbors of $x$ and $y$ (with some vertices taken in each copy of the largest component), which both form independent sets. This implies that any edge incident to $w$ is not part of a triangle, contradicting the assumption that each edge in $G$ is in some triangle. See Figure \ref{Gandtriangle} for a special case of this construction.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $G$ be an oriented graph such that every edge belongs to an oriented triangle. If there exists an edge $\overrightarrow{uv} \in E(G)$ such that $\deg(u) = \deg(v) = 2$, then
    \[\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,G) = \Theta(n \log n).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: It follows as a direct application of Lemma \ref{sat_nlogn}. Figure \ref{Gandtriangle} shows how a host graph with $\Theta(n \log n)$ edges can be constructed for such graphs.
head: environment

label: bip nlogn upper
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First observe that $G$ is non-bipartite, as it contains a triangle. We use the same construction of the host graph $H$ as in Lemma \ref{ssat_nlogn} with distinguished edge $\overrightarrow{uv}$, which semisaturates $G$. It remains to show that $H$ avoids $G$. By assumption, the graph obtained from $G$ by removing the edge $\overrightarrow{uv}$ is bipartite. We can partition its vertices into $B$ and $W$. Since $N_G(u) \cap N_G(v)$ is non-empty, we know that $u$ and $v$ are in the same part, wlog. $B$. Then, it follows that $N = (N_G(u) \cup N_G(v)) \setminus \{u,v\} \subseteq W$.

    Following the construction in Lemma \ref{ssat_nlogn}, we take $k$ copies of the graph $G^{uv} = G \setminus \{u,v\}$ and $n'$ isolated vertices. Then, for each copy of $G^{uv}$, we take the corresponding set $N$ and connect it to the isolated vertices. Since all the vertices of $N$ are in $W$, we can take the isolated vertices to be in $B$. This preserves the bipartiteness of the host graph $H$. As $G$ is non-bipartite, it follows that $H$ contains no copy of $G$.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
For $s \ge 1$,
    \[\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,D_s)=\Theta(n \log n).\]
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
For $s \ge 1$,
    \[\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,W_s)=\Theta(n).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to construct a host graph with a linear number of edges. Let $X_{s}$ be a tournament on vertex set $V(X_s) = \{v_{1}, \dots, v_{2s+1}\}$ and edge set \[E(X_s) = \{\overrightarrow{v_{i}v_{j}} : 1 \leq j - i \leq s \pmod{2s+1}\}.\] 

    Let $H$ be a host graph on $n$ vertices obtained from a disjoint union of $\lfloor \frac{n}{2s+1} \rfloor$ copies of $X_{s}$ and an independent set $I$ of isolated vertices.

    Notice that $H$ avoids $W_s$ because there exists a vertex in $W_s$ with outdegree $s+1$, while the maximum outdegree in $H$ is $s$. On the other hand, we want to show that adding any edge within $H \setminus I$ creates a copy of $W_s$. By symmetry, it suffices to consider an edge going out of the vertex $v_k$, for $1 \leq k \leq 2s+1$. We want to argue that the subgraph induced by the vertices $v_k, \dots, v_{k+s+1}$ contains a copy of $D_s$. By the construction of $X_{s}$, there is a $2$-path $v_k \rightarrow v_i \rightarrow v_{k+s+1}$ for every $i \in \{k+1, \dots, k+s\}$. Moreover, $\overrightarrow{v_{k+s+1}v_{k}} \in E(X_{s})$, which indeed forms a copy of $D_s$. We can greedily add linearly many edges from $I$, until the host graph fully saturates $W_s$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: For $s\ge 2$, \[\mathrm{sat}_{\mathrel{\scalebox{0.75}[1]{$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$}}}(n,Q_s)=\Theta(n\sqrt{\log n}).\footnote{The saturation function of $Q_1$ is linear, as follows from the same construction used for $W_1$.}\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove the lower bound. Let $H$ be an $n$-vertex host graph saturating $Q_s$, with vertex set $V$. We denote by $D_s$ the graph obtained from $Q_s$ by deleting the leaf vertex and the incident edge. An \emph{instar} is the graph obtained from $D_s$ by deleting its top vertex, which is adjacent to the leaf vertex of $Q_s$. The unique vertex of indegree $s$ in an incherry is called its \emph{center}.
    
    Every non-edge plays the role of some edge in a copy of $Q_s$ once it is added to $H$. Let $V_1$ consist of those vertices that are incident to a non-edge that can serve as the hanging edge of a copy of $Q_s$ in which this vertex is not the leaf vertex of this copy of $Q_s$. Note that the vertices of $V_1$ have indegree exactly one, since a larger indegree would create a copy of $Q_s$ in $H$. 

    Let $V_2 = V \setminus V_1$. By the definition of $V_1$, for each $v\in V_1$, there exists a copy of $D_i$ in $H$ such that $v$ corresponds to its top vertex, and there is an instar on the remaining $s+1$ vertices of this copy of $D_s$. Note that while for a given $v_1\in V_1$, this instar might not be unique, its center is unique. For simplicity, we can fix one such instar for each vertex of $V_1$.

    First, we claim that every vertex belonging to one of these instars must be in $V_2$. Indeed, if an instar contained a vertex of $V_1$, using the fact that every vertex $V_1$ has indegree exactly $1$, we obtain a copy of $Q_s$. See the rightmost figure of Figure \ref{fig:incherries} for $s=2$.
    
    Second, we claim that each edge $e$ is an edge of at most $s-1$ defined above instars. Indeed, each such instar contains an oriented triangle through $e$. If there are $s$ instars through $e$, then there would be $s$ oriented triangles. Together with an additional edge from one of these instars playing the role of the leaf, we would get a copy of $Q_s$, which is a contradiction. See Figure \ref{fig:incherries} for $s=2$.

    \begin{figure}[ht]
    	\centering
    	\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth]{instars.pdf}
    	\caption{\label{fig:incherries} If an edge is in at least $s=2$ instars (left and middle figure) or if one instar has a vertex $v_2$ in $V_1$ (right figure), then $H$ contains $Q_s$ (red).}
    \end{figure}

    Observe that within $V_2$, no non-edge can be saturated such that it serves as the hanging edge of $Q_s$. Hence, for every non-edge in $V_2$, adding this edge would create a copy of $D_s$. By Corollary \ref{cor:subsat}, $H$ has $\Omega(|V_2|\log |V_2|)$ edges. If $|V_2|=\Omega(n/\sqrt{\log n})$, then we are done. 
    
    From now on, we may assume that $N=|V_2|=O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$. 
    For each vertex of $V_2$, let $a_i$ denote the number of instars defined above that have this vertex as their center, and order these numbers so that
    \[a_1\le a_2\le \dots \le a_{N}\le \frac{(s-1)(N-1)}{s}.\]
    The last inequality follows because each instar consists of $s$ edges, all contained in $V_2$, and each edge belongs to at most $s-1$ instars. Since we fixed exactly one instar for each vertex of $V_1$, we have
    \[\sum_{1 \leq i \leq N} a_i = |V_1| = n-N.\] 
    Moreover, since $N=O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$, we have $n-N\ge n/2$ for all sufficiently large $n$. 
    
    We claim that for any pair of vertices $w_i, w_j\in V_2$, with incident instars corresponding to some $v_i,v_j\in V_1$, respectively, if $\overrightarrow{w_jw_i}\notin E(H)$, then $w_j$ and $v_i$ must be adjacent in $H$. Indeed, otherwise, the non-edge $\overrightarrow{v_iw_j}$ needs to be saturated. Adding this edge cannot serve as the leaf edge of a copy of $Q_s$ (as $w_j$ is in $V_2$). Thus, it must complete an oriented triangle, which would use the edge $\overrightarrow{w_iv_i}$, as $v_1$ has indegree one. This would require an edge $\overrightarrow{w_jw_i}$ in $H$, which does not exist. See Figure \ref{fig:wiwjforceedge}.

    \begin{figure}[ht]
    	\centering
    	\includegraphics[width=0.4\textwidth]{wiwjforceedge.pdf}
    	\caption{\label{fig:wiwjforceedge} No edge from $w_i$ to $w_j$ forces an edge $v_iw_j$ in $H$.}
    \end{figure}

    For a fixed vertex $w_i$, there are $a_i$ corresponding vertices in $V_1$. Since there cannot be an edge oriented in both directions between $w_i$ and $w_j$, the previous argument implies that there are at least $\min \{a_i,a_j\}$ edges between $V_1$ and $\{w_i,w_j\}$. Therefore, the number of edges between $V_1$ and $V_2$ is at least $\sum_{1\le i<j\le N}\min \{a_i,a_j\}$. We are left to give a lower bound to \[A=\sum_{1\le i<j\le N}\min \{a_i,a_j\} = (N-1)a_1+(N-2)a_2+\dots 2a_{N-2}+a_{N-1}.\]
        
    Recall that for large enough $n$, we have $\sum a_i\ge  n/2$, and $a_N\le N\le cn/\sqrt{\log n}$ for some constant $c$. Assuming only these, we get that the sum $A$ is smallest when $N$ is as large as possible, i.e., $N=\lfloor cn/\sqrt{\log n}\rfloor$, and the $a_i$ are $0$ up to some point, after which they are all equal to $N$ (with one possible exception). In this case, we have at least $x= \lfloor n/(2N)\rfloor$ values of $a_i$ that are equal to $N$. At least $\lfloor x/2\rfloor-1$ of them are multiplied by a factor of at least $\lfloor x/2\rfloor$ in $A$. Consequently,
    \[A \geq \lfloor x/2\rfloor(\lfloor x/2\rfloor-1) N = \Omega(n^2/N) = \Omega (n\sqrt{\log n}).\] 
    Hence, the host graph $H$ contains at least this many edges, finishing the proof of the lower bound.
\bigskip    

    We now present the construction showing the matching upper bound. The idea is to provide a construction for which the upper bound would be tight at each step. First, we saturate all non-edges in some subset $V_1 \subseteq V$ that contains most vertices. Then, we saturate most non-edges in the remaining set, as done in Lemma \ref{ssat_nlogn}, using only a small set of vertices so that we do not need to make further iterations.

    We first construct an almost saturating graph $H_0$ on $n$ vertices, in which all but a few non-edges are saturated in both orientations. The desired saturated graph $H$ is then obtained by greedily orienting the remaining non-edges until the graph becomes saturated.

    \begin{figure}[ht]
        \centering
        \includegraphics[width=1\linewidth]{nsqrtn-constr-3.pdf}
        \caption{The host graph $H_0$ that (almost) saturates $Q_3$.}
        \label{fig:diamondplus}
    \end{figure}

    For the structure of $H_0$, see Figure \ref{fig:diamondplus}, which shows the case $s=2$, the general case being similar. We may assume that $n$ is large enough.
    Let $y=\lceil \sqrt{\log n}\rceil $ and let $V_2\subset V $ such that $|V_2|=y$.
    We partition the remaining vertices into disjoint sets $V_1$, $V_3$, and $X$ such that $|V_3|$ is divisible by $s$ and 
    \[ y\cdot |V_3|\frac{s-1}{s}=|V_1|,
    \qquad
    |X|<(s-1)y+s.\]
    This can be easily done by starting with $V_1=V\setminus V_2$ and moving vertices from $V_1$ to $V_3$ in sets of size $s$, as long as $y\cdot|V_3|(s-1)/s\le |V_1|$. We stop just before this would become false. Note that at this point for $x=|V_1|-y\cdot|V_3|(s-1)/s$, we have $0\le x < (s-1)y+s=O(\sqrt {\log n})$. Now take $x$ vertices from $V_1$ to form $X$. Finally, note that 
    \[|V_3|\le \frac{ns}{(s-1)y} \le \frac{2n}{\sqrt{\log n}}.\]
    
    We now define the edges of $H_0$. We add every edge between $V_3$ and $V_2$, oriented towards $V_2$. We partition the vertices of $V_3$ into sets of size $s$ that we call \emph{groups}. The number of sets consisting of a vertex from $V_2$ and a group from $V_3$ is $y|V_3|/s=|V_1|/(s-1)$. Consequently, we can assign each vertex $v\in V_1$ to one such set so that every set is assigned exactly $s-1$ times. Fix such an assignment.
    
    For each $v\in V_1$, we add the edge from the vertex assigned to $v$ in $V_2$ oriented towards $v$ and $s$ edges oriented from $v$ to all vertices of the group in $V_3$ assigned to $v$. Thus, we obtain a copy of $D_s$ on these $s+2$ vertices, one copy for each $v\in V_1$. Notice that each vertex in $V_1$ has indegree $1$ and outdegree $s$. Moreover, the complete bipartite graph between $V_2$ and $V_3$ is oriented towards $V_2$, and each of its edges belongs to exactly $s-1$ of the copies of $D_s$ defined above.

    The sets $V_1$ and $V_2$ each remain independent in $H$. It remains to define the edges inside $V_3$. As in the proofs of Lemma \ref{ssat_nlogn} and Lemma \ref{sat_nlogn}, we construct a graph on $V_3$ that saturates $D_s$ while avoiding $Q_s$.

    To this end, let $z=2s\lceil \log |V_3|\rceil$. Let $V_3^{b}$ be the set formed by $z/s$ groups of $V_3$, and let $V_3^{a} = V_3 \setminus V_3^b$.
    Now define $\lceil \log |V_3|\rceil=z/(2s)$ partitions of $V_3^a$ into two sets such that every pair of vertices in $V_3^a$ is separated by at least one of these partitions. For each bipartition $A\cup B=V_3^a$, assign $2$ groups of $V_3^b$ such that no vertex is assigned twice. Connect all vertices of $A$ with the first group of vertices oriented towards the first group. Similarly, connect all vertices of $B$ with the second group oriented towards the second group of vertices. Also, add all edges from the first group towards $B$ and from the second group towards $A$. This forms a complete bipartite graph between $V_3^a$ and the $2s$ vertices of $B$ in these two groups. Repeating this construction for every bipartition, we get a complete bipartite graph with parts $V_3^a$ and $V_3^b$. See Figure \ref{fig:diamondplus}. 

    We added $O(n)$ edges between $V_2$ and $V_3$, $O(n)$ edges between $V_1$ and $V_2\cup V_3$, and \[|V_3^a||V_3^b|=O(|V_3|\log |V_3|)=O(n\sqrt{\log n})\] edges within $V_3$, since $|V_3|\le ns/\sqrt{\log n}$. Thus, $H_0$ has $O(n\sqrt{\log n})$ edges in total.

    Next, we show that $H_0$ avoids $Q_s$. Assume the contrary, that $H_0$ contains a copy of $Q_s$. Observe that $Q_s$ contains $s$ oriented triangles. The subgraph induced by $V_3$ is bipartite, and all edges between $V_2$ and $V_3$ are oriented towards the independent set $V_2$. Hence, the subgraph induced by $V_2\cup V_3$ contains no oriented triangles.
    
    Therefore, some vertex $v\in V_1$ is in this copy of $Q_s$, and thus the oriented triangle through $v$ must have its other two vertices in $V_2$ and $V_3$, respectively. Since every edge between $V_2$ and $V_3$ is contained in exactly $s-1$ oriented triangles, the edge of $Q_s$ that lies in $s$ oriented triangles must be incident to $v$. Yet, the edge from $v$ to $V_3$ has only one oriented triangle through it, so the edge from $V_2$ to $v$ must be the edge of $Q_s$ contained in two oriented triangles. Notice that this edge has exactly $s$ oriented triangles through it, so the $D_s$ part of this $Q_s$ must be exactly the $D_s$ we put on $v$ in this construction phase. But then $v$ must have indegree at least $2$, contradicting the fact that $v$ has indegree exactly $1$. 

    Finally, we prove that almost all non-edges are saturated in $H_0$. We distinguish three possible cases: 
    
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item Suppose that we add a new edge oriented towards a vertex $v\in V_1$. Together with the copy of $D_s$ associated with $v$ and its assigned $(s+1)$-set, this creates a copy of $Q_s$.
    
    \item Suppose that we add a new edge $\overrightarrow{v_1v_3}$, where $v_1\in V_1$ and $v_3\in V_3$. There is a unique edge from some $v_2\in V_2$ such that $\overrightarrow{v_2v_1}\in E(H_0)$. Moreover, there exist $s-1$ vertices $v_1^1,v_1^2,\dots v_1^{s-1}\in V_1$ such that their assigned $s+1$-set is the same and contains the vertices $v_2$ and $v_3$. Thus, there are $s-1$ oriented triangles in $H_1$ through $\overrightarrow{v_2v_3}$. The added edge creates an additional oriented triangle on $v_1,v_3,v_2$, and we obtain a copy of $D_s$. With an appropriate $v_3'\in V_3$, $v_3'\ne v_3$ that has an edge oriented towards $v_2$, we get a copy of $Q_s$.
    
    \item Suppose that we add a new edge $\overrightarrow{ab}$ with $a,b\in V_3^a$. Choose one of the bipartitions $A\cup B=V_3^a$ constructed above that separates $a$ and $b$. There are two groups associated with this bipartition, one of them together with $a$ and $b$, forms a copy of $D_s$. Taking an additional vertex from $V_1$ that has an edge oriented towards $b$, we obtain a copy of $Q_s$.
    \end{enumerate}

    Thus, the only non-edges that may remain unsaturated are
    $O(n\sqrt{\log n})$ non-edges incident to $X$,
    $O(n\sqrt{\log n})$ non-edges between $V_1$ and $V_2$, $O(\log^2 n)$ non-edges within $V_2$, and $O(\log^2 n)$ non-edges within $V_3^b$.
    In total, this is $O(n\sqrt{\log n})$. We can then greedily add edges to get $H$, finishing the proof.

    It might be tempting to think about Lemma \ref{ver_trans} in the opposite direction. We take any connected graph, and we want to complete it into a vertex-transitive graph. The main question that arises is: how small (in terms of the number of vertices) can such a vertex-transitive graph be?
